profiles.meeting_scenario: A weekly coordination meeting at a tertiary cancer center between the gynecologic oncology service and the nurse navigation program, held as part of launching a standardized care-coordination workflow for women with ovarian, uterine, and cervical cancers. The team is adapting findings from a rapid review into local practice by aligning how multidisciplinary tumor board decisions, patient follow-up tasks, and survivorship materials move between clinicians and coordinators. The agenda is to confirm the handoff points after tumor board, agree on what goes into the shared care plan, review who updates patients after major treatment-plan changes, and synchronize the list of patients to be tracked for the next month's pilot. The expected outcome is a shared understanding of interfaces between physician decision-making and navigation tasks so the pilot can begin next week without revising the core workflow.

members.name: Dr. Elena Marquez
members.role: Gynecologic Oncologist and Tumor Board Lead
members.expertise: Surgical and medical management of gynecologic malignancies, multidisciplinary treatment planning, tumor board operations
members.background: A senior attending physician at a large academic hospital who has led the weekly gynecologic oncology tumor board for three years and is responsible for standardizing physician-facing documentation across inpatient and outpatient oncology services.
members.private_state: She wants the pilot to start on schedule with minimal extra documentation burden on physicians, and she is especially concerned that coordination steps not slow down treatment starts for newly diagnosed patients.
hidden_assumptions: When the team says a case is 'reviewed at tumor board,' that means the recommendation has been entered into the official physician note and is ready for downstream coordination.
The 'care plan' for coordination purposes is the oncology treatment plan visible in the EHR problem-oriented oncology module, not a separate patient-facing packet.
A patient is 'scheduled for follow-up' once the clinic request has been placed, even if the actual appointment time has not yet been confirmed with the patient.

If navigation is asked to 'close the loop' with the patient, that communication happens through the routine nurse callback workflow documented in the chart, not necessarily through a separate survivorship or education encounter.

members.name: Rachel Kim
members.expertise: Care coordination, patient education, cross-service scheduling, survivorship transitions, telephone triage
members.background: An experienced oncology nurse navigator who supports patients from diagnosis through treatment transitions, coordinates referrals and follow-ups across surgery, infusion, radiation, and supportive services, and has recently been asked to help operationalize a more standardized coordination model.
members.private_state: She wants the new workflow to prevent patients from falling through gaps after treatment decisions, and she is particularly focused on making sure the pilot includes actionable scheduling confirmation and understandable patient-facing summaries.
hidden_assumptions: When a case is 'reviewed at tumor board,' the recommendation is actionable for navigation once it is verbally finalized in the meeting, even if the attending note is entered later.

The 'care plan' should include the navigator's integrated patient-facing roadmap with appointments, referrals, expected next steps, and contact guidance, not just the physician treatment plan in the EHR.
A patient is only truly 'scheduled for follow-up' when the patient has a booked date/time and knows where and with whom the visit will occur.

To 'close the loop' means ensuring the patient directly understands the updated plan and barriers have been addressed, usually through a navigator call and checklist rather than relying on standard physician-team callbacks alone.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to put the next steps into the 'care plan.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the clinician-facing oncology treatment plan documented in the EHR, centered on diagnosis, regimen, and intended treatment sequence.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a broader navigator-maintained coordination document that includes appointments, referrals, patient instructions, and practical next steps.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In oncology settings, 'care plan' is a familiar umbrella term used across clinical, administrative, and patient-education contexts, so both can nod along without noticing they are anchoring to different artifacts.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that high-risk patients need 'scheduled follow-up' within 72 hours after treatment-plan changes.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks the standard is met once staff place the follow-up order or routing request within 72 hours, because the clinic scheduling queue then owns the next step.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks the standard is met only when the patient has an actual confirmed appointment or documented direct contact if an appointment is still pending.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are using the same quality-improvement language and share the same intent of timely follow-up, but they silently apply different operational thresholds drawn from their own workflows.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both talk about using 'the board list' to identify pilot patients and handoffs.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is referring to the finalized tumor board agenda exported the night before the meeting from the physician coordinator's spreadsheet, which includes only cases formally submitted with complete pathology and imaging.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is referring to the navigator's running shared patient tracker labeled 'board list,' which includes tentative add-ons, post-board follow-ups, and patients expected to be discussed soon.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both lists are locally known by the same shorthand, overlap heavily in patient names, and are routinely used in adjacent workflows, so the naming collision feels normal rather than suspicious.

misalignment_points.topic: How to 'close the loop' after board recommendations
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree navigation should 'close the loop' after major tumor board decisions.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes navigation will monitor the chart, see the signed note, and rely on standard service callbacks unless a specific social barrier is flagged.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes navigation will proactively call the patient, reconcile referrals and logistics, and document a dedicated coordination contact after each major change.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds like shared commitment to completion rather than a method choice, and each person treats their own workflow as the obvious default implementation.

turns.inner_thought: We are too close to launch to reopen the whole design. What I need today is a clean handoff from tumor board into the chart so navigation can work off the documented recommendation without creating extra physician steps. If we keep this tied to the existing note and callback workflows, we can start next week and avoid delaying treatment starts for new patients.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. My main goal today is to line up the handoffs from tumor board into navigation so we can start the pilot next week without adding friction. If we can agree on where recommendations land, who picks them up, and how we track the follow-through, that should be enough to move.

turns.inner_thought: I need to make sure the pilot includes the patients on my running board list, not just the ones formally presented, because the gaps usually happen around add-ons, pending discussions, and immediate post-board coordination. If we only track the narrow formal agenda, we'll miss the exact people who need navigation most.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. From my side, I want to be sure the pilot captures the patients on the board list who are most likely to need cross-service coordination, especially when the plan is changing quickly.

turns.inner_thought: Good, we can anchor this to the finalized board list from the coordinator's spreadsheet pull the night before. That's the cleanest denominator and it keeps eligibility tied to cases that were actually submitted with complete information. We do not need a moving target during the pilot.
turns.utterance: Agreed. We can use the board list from the coordinator's pull to define who comes into the pilot each week, and then build the handoffs from there.

turns.inner_thought: Once the recommendation is settled in the meeting, I want the care plan to function as the shared roadmap everyone can follow—appointments, referrals, next steps, practical instructions. That way radiation, infusion, and social work don't each have to reconstruct what is supposed to happen.
turns.utterance: One thing that would help is that once a case is reviewed, the next steps go into the care plan so radiation, infusion, and social work are all looking at the same roadmap.

turns.inner_thought: That's fine as long as the attending updates the oncology treatment plan in the EHR after board and the chart reflects the recommendation in the official note. Then the downstream teams can see the plan without us inventing another document. Navigation can follow from the chart once it's in place.
turns.utterance: Yes, that works. The attending can make sure the care plan is updated after board so the downstream team has the recommendation.

turns.inner_thought: For the highest-risk cases, I need a real safeguard. 'Scheduled follow-up' has to mean the patient actually has a date and time, or at minimum we've directly reached them if scheduling is still in progress. Otherwise patients can sit for days assuming someone will call.
turns.utterance: And for the high-risk patients, I'd really like us to set the expectation that they have scheduled follow-up within 72 hours after a treatment-plan change, so nobody is left sitting with something unacted on.

turns.inner_thought: Seventy-two hours is reasonable if the clinic places the request promptly after the note is signed. Once the order or routing is in, scheduling owns it, and that should satisfy the standard without creating a manual chase for physicians. The signed note remains the trigger.
turns.utterance: I think 72 hours is reasonable. The clinic can place the follow-up requests right after the note is signed, and that should give us a reliable path for scheduled follow-up.

turns.inner_thought: Good. I am assuming navigation will actively call after major decisions, especially new chemo starts and multi-referral cases, and make sure the patient understands what is happening next. That's what closing the loop requires if we actually want to prevent drop-off.
turns.utterance: That helps. On our end, navigation can close the loop after those major decisions, especially for new chemotherapy starts and for patients who need several referrals moving at once.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect—if navigation is watching for the signed recommendation and making sure nothing unusual gets missed, then the standard callback flow can handle most routine communication. I do not want every board change to generate a separate extra encounter unless there's a barrier.
turns.utterance: Good. That should stay fairly efficient, because once the board recommendation is in the chart, the usual callback flow already covers most patients.

turns.inner_thought: I'll keep using my tracker—the board list—as the live operational view, and I'll mark the care plan status there along with whether follow-up is truly scheduled. That should let me see who still needs a call, a booked visit, or unresolved referrals.
turns.utterance: I can keep tracking progress on the board list and use the care plan to flag whether follow-up has been scheduled, so we have a quick read on what is still pending.

turns.inner_thought: This sounds aligned enough to proceed. Physicians will document the treatment plan, navigation will pick up the rest through their normal processes, and the pilot population will be based on the weekly formal board agenda. We do not need to spend another week refining wording.
turns.utterance: Great. So at a high level: the physicians will update the care plan, navigation will close the loop, and the pilot cohort will come from the weekly board list. If we hold to that, I think we're in good shape to start.

turns.inner_thought: Okay, I'll get my tracker ready for next week and watch for the first set of patients who need direct coordination after board. I still want to make sure scheduled follow-up really happens, but we can work that in once cases start coming through.
turns.utterance: Sounds good. I'll prep my tracker for next week and keep an eye out for the first group needing scheduled follow-up after board.
